https://www.baltictimes.com/baltic_minis.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Baltic ministers sign energy reserve deal, discuss grid security 2026-07-22 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Baltic energy ministers agreed in Riga on Wednesday to jointly strengthen energy system reserve capacities and discussed sharing emergency power grid equipment. Energy Minister Lukas Savickas and his Latvian and Estonian counterparts signed a declaration under which the countries will jointly assess the need for transformers, transmission towers, generators and other emergency equipment required in the event of threats or failures. "Joint reserves and an agreement to coordinate actions during emergencies will help ensure a more reliable energy supply for the public, while joint decisions will allow for more efficient and cost-effective strengthening of energy infrastructure security," Savickas said. The countries' transmission system operators are expected, after assessing their needs, to jointly apply for European Union funding for the purchase and maintenance of reserve capacities. The ministers also discussed the protection of strategic energy facilities. According to the ministry, the ministers emphasised that drones have "become a new security reality" and that protection against them is an "integral part of critical infrastructure protection at the regional level". The agreement comes amid growing concerns over potential threats to critical infrastructure. Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries have warned of possible Russian provocations, while President Gitanas Nauseda has said that critical transport and energy infrastructure in Lithuania could become targets. Since June, the Lithuanian military has been assisting in the protection of key energy sites, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipeda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection switchyard in Alytus, a transformer substation and the Kruonis pumped storage hydroelectric plant. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, AndrÃ¡s Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg By Nick Thorpe in Hungary Published 11 August 2026 Hungary's parliament has elected AndrÃ¡s Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state. The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous. His task will be to monitor Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace OrbÃ¡n's constitution of 2011. "We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," AndrÃ¡s Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6. "The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs." All 51 MPs belonging to OrbÃ¡n's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, TamÃ¡s Sulyok, from the post last month . In his speech, AndrÃ¡s Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution. Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking OrbÃ¡n's legacy. Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution. The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which OrbÃ¡n used to govern by decree, were all cancelled. The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government. Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law. Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July , as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs. Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored. If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening. In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives. Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. "I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking." Baka was elected today as a transitional figure. Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible, the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years. Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders. "The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people." Related topics Hungary More on this story What does new Hungarian PM PÃ©ter Magyar stand for?
